stills.heading: Degrees, Chords and Tonality
stills.caption: Lesson 5 · Harmony Course · Storm Studios Learning
stills.narration: Hello, and welcome back to Storm Studios Learning. In the previous lesson we built fifth chords on every degree of the basic scales. Before we start writing for the vocal quartet, we need to complete a few ideas about degrees, chords and tonality.

stills.heading: An explanatory lesson
stills.caption: Everything we see today will be used in the following lessons
stills.narration: This is an explanatory lesson. It has no assignment for the Virtual Teacher, but everything we see today will be used in the following lessons.

stills.heading: The names of the degrees
stills.caption: C major
stills.narration: Let's start with the names of the degrees. Each degree of the scale has its own name. We will see them in C major.

stills.heading: Tonic
stills.caption: The center of the key
stills.narration: The first degree is the tonic. It is the center of the key.

stills.heading: Dominant
stills.caption: A fifth above the tonic
stills.narration: The fifth degree, a fifth above the tonic, is the dominant.

stills.heading: Subdominant
stills.caption: A fifth below the tonic
stills.narration: And a fifth below the tonic we have the fourth degree, the subdominant.

stills.heading: Mediant
stills.caption: Halfway between tonic and dominant
stills.narration: The third degree, halfway between the tonic and the dominant, is called the mediant.

stills.heading: Submediant
stills.caption: Halfway between tonic and subdominant, going down
stills.narration: And halfway between the tonic and the subdominant, but going down, we have the sixth degree, the submediant.

stills.heading: Supertonic
stills.caption: Just above the tonic
stills.narration: The second degree, just above the tonic, is the supertonic.

stills.heading: A mirror around the tonic
stills.narration: Notice how the names mirror each other around the tonic: the dominant above and the subdominant below; the mediant above and the submediant below.

stills.heading: Seventh degree: leading tone
stills.caption: A half step below the tonic
stills.narration: We still need the seventh degree. When the seventh degree is a half step below the tonic, as in the major scale and in harmonic minor, we call it the leading tone.

stills.heading: Subtonic
stills.caption: A whole step below the tonic
stills.narration: But in the natural minor scale, the seventh degree is a whole step below the tonic. In that case we call it the subtonic.

stills.heading: A natural minor
stills.caption: G is the subtonic
stills.narration: For example, in A natural minor, G is the subtonic.

stills.heading: A harmonic minor
stills.caption: G♯ is the leading tone
stills.narration: In A harmonic minor, G sharp is the leading tone.

stills.heading: Functions of the degrees
stills.caption: Tonal · modal · secondary · attractive
stills.narration: Now let's look at the functions of the degrees.

stills.heading: Tonal or principal degrees
stills.caption: I · IV · V
stills.narration: The first, fourth and fifth degrees are the tonal, or principal, degrees. They are the ones that hold the key together.

stills.heading: Modal degrees
stills.caption: III · VI
stills.narration: The third and sixth degrees are the modal degrees, because they tell us whether we are in major or in minor.

stills.heading: Secondary degrees
stills.caption: II · III · VI · VII
stills.narration: The secondary degrees are all those that are not principal: the second, the third, the sixth and the seventh.

stills.heading: Attractive degrees
stills.caption: They require a special resolution
stills.narration: And then we have the attractive degrees. We call a note attractive when its harmonic tendency requires a special resolution.

stills.heading: The leading tone
stills.caption: The most important attractive note
stills.narration: The most important attractive note is the leading tone.

stills.heading: IV and VI with the leading tone
stills.caption: F and A in the same chord as B
stills.narration: The fourth and sixth degrees also become attractive when they appear in the same chord as the leading tone.

stills.heading: Modal attractive degrees
stills.narration: We also consider attractive three altered degrees that come from the modes.

stills.heading: Phrygian II · D♭
stills.narration: The Phrygian second degree. In C, it is D flat.

stills.heading: Lydian IV · F♯
stills.narration: The Lydian fourth degree. In C, it is F sharp.

stills.heading: Mixolydian VII · B♭
stills.narration: And the Mixolydian seventh degree. In C, it is B flat.

stills.heading: Review the modes
stills.caption: Lesson 2
stills.narration: If you want to review the modes, go back to lesson two.

stills.heading: The chord
stills.caption: Any simultaneity of different sounds
stills.narration: Now let's move on to chords. In the previous lesson we said that a chord is any simultaneity of different sounds.

stills.heading: Stacked thirds
stills.caption: Built from the root
stills.narration: And that we build it from a generating sound, the root, by stacking thirds.

stills.heading: Fifth chord
stills.caption: Two thirds
stills.narration: With two thirds we get the fifth chord, which you already know.

stills.heading: Seventh chord
stills.caption: Three thirds
stills.narration: If we stack three thirds, we get the seventh chord.

stills.heading: Ninth chord
stills.caption: Four thirds
stills.narration: With four thirds, the ninth chord.

stills.heading: Eleventh chord
stills.caption: Five thirds
stills.narration: With five, the eleventh chord.

stills.heading: Thirteenth chord
stills.caption: Six thirds
stills.narration: And with six thirds, the thirteenth chord.

stills.heading: The name comes from the highest note
stills.caption: Interval between the root and the highest note
stills.narration: The name always comes from the interval between the root and the highest note of the chord.

stills.heading: Chords in thirds on C
stills.narration: Let's listen to the five chords on C.

stills.heading: Harmony
stills.caption: Intervallic structure of chords and the laws of their connection
stills.narration: Let's also remember that harmony studies the intervallic structure of chords and the laws by which they are connected.

stills.heading: Harmonies, in plural
stills.caption: Period · genre · stylistic movement · composer
stills.narration: And that we speak of harmonies, in plural, because those laws change with the period, the genre, the stylistic movement and the composer.

stills.heading: The harmonic series
stills.caption: Whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency
stills.narration: The harmonic series helps us understand that history. When a note sounds, we don't only hear its fundamental frequency, but a whole series of natural harmonics, which are whole-number multiples of that frequency.

stills.heading: Harmonic series on C
stills.narration: This is the harmonic series on C.

stills.heading: Harmonic 2: the octave
stills.narration: The second harmonic is the octave.

stills.heading: Harmonic 3: the fifth
stills.narration: The third, the fifth.

stills.heading: Harmonic 4: the octave again
stills.narration: The fourth, the octave again.

stills.heading: Harmonic 5: the major third
stills.narration: The fifth harmonic is the major third.

stills.heading: Harmonics 1 to 6: a major chord
stills.narration: With the first six harmonics we already have a complete major chord.

stills.heading: Harmonic 7: a flat B♭
stills.narration: The seventh harmonic is a B flat slightly lower than the one on the piano. That is why we say it is flat.

stills.heading: Flat ↓ and sharp ↑
stills.narration: Other harmonics also sound slightly lower or slightly higher than the note we use to write them. The arrows show this.

stills.heading: Harmonies through history
stills.narration: Throughout history, Western music has gradually accepted as consonant harmonics that lie further and further along this series. Let's walk through that history with an example from each stage.

stills.musicCredit: Hildegard von Bingen — Canticles of Ecstasy
stills.heading: Monody
stills.caption: Harmonics 1 and 2
stills.narration: First, monody: a single melodic line. It corresponds to harmonics one and two, the fundamental and its octave. Let's listen.

stills.heading: Organum
stills.caption: Harmonics 3 and 4
stills.narration: Next comes organum, which adds parallel voices in fifths and fourths. These are harmonics three and four. Let's listen.

stills.musicCredit: Palestrina — Missa Papae Marcelli · Dresdner Kammerchor
stills.heading: Ars Nova
stills.caption: Harmonics 5 and 6
stills.narration: With the Ars Nova, in the fourteenth century, and later in the Renaissance, the third is added, and with it the complete chord. These are harmonics five and six. Let's listen.

stills.musicCredit: J. S. Bach — “O Haupt voll Blut und Wunden”, St Matthew Passion
stills.heading: Pre-Classical
stills.caption: Harmonics 7 and 8 · Bach · Handel · Mozart · Beethoven
stills.narration: In the pre-classical period, from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century, with Bach, Handel, Mozart and Beethoven, the seventh appears. These are harmonics seven and eight. Let's listen.

stills.musicCredit: Chopin — Prelude in E minor, Op. 28 No. 4
stills.heading: Classical and Romantic
stills.caption: Harmonics 9 and 10 · Schubert · Chopin · Brahms
stills.narration: Then come Schubert, Chopin and Brahms, who appear in our chart as the classical and romantic period. Their harmony reaches harmonics nine and ten, the ninth. Let's listen.

stills.heading: Twentieth century
stills.caption: Harmonics 11 to 20
stills.narration: From the eleventh to the twentieth harmonic we find three twentieth-century movements.

stills.musicCredit: Debussy — La cathédrale engloutie, Préludes, Book 1
stills.heading: Impressionism
stills.caption: Debussy · Ravel · Fauré · Satie
stills.narration: Impressionism, with Debussy, Ravel, Fauré and Satie. Let's listen.

stills.heading: Expressionism
stills.caption: Stravinsky · Shostakovich · Bartók · Scriabin
stills.narration: Expressionism, with Stravinsky, Shostakovich, Bartók and Scriabin. Let's listen.

stills.heading: Dodecaphony
stills.caption: Schoenberg · Berg · Webern · Hindemith
stills.narration: And dodecaphony, with Schoenberg, Berg and Webern, which uses all twelve tones without a tonal center. Hindemith also appears in the chart. Let's listen.

stills.heading: Microtonalism
stills.caption: Harmonics 21 to 24 · Julián Carrillo
stills.narration: Finally, beyond the twentieth harmonic, microtonalism uses intervals smaller than a half step. Its great pioneer was the Mexican composer Julián Carrillo, with his Sonido Trece. Let's listen.

stills.heading: Four types of fifth chords
stills.caption: Major or minor by the third; augmented or diminished by the fifth
stills.narration: Now let's go back to fifth chords. If we take each degree of the basic scales as a root, we only get four types of chords: major, minor, diminished and augmented. A chord is major or minor because of its third, and augmented or diminished because of its fifth.

stills.heading: Tonal regions
stills.narration: The chords of a scale are grouped into three tonal regions: the subdominant region, the tonic region and the dominant region.

stills.heading: One principal and two secondary chords
stills.caption: The secondary chords, a third above and below
stills.narration: Each region has a principal chord that gives it its name, and two secondary chords, a third above and a third below it.

stills.heading: C major arranged in thirds
stills.narration: If we arrange the chords of C major in thirds, it becomes very clear.

stills.heading: Subdominant region
stills.caption: IV principal · II and VI secondary
stills.narration: The subdominant region has the fourth degree as its principal chord, and the second and sixth as secondary chords.

stills.heading: Tonic region
stills.caption: I principal · VI and III secondary
stills.narration: The tonic region has the first degree, with the sixth and the third.

stills.heading: Dominant region
stills.caption: V principal · III and VII secondary
stills.narration: And the dominant region has the fifth degree, with the third and the seventh.

stills.heading: III and VI: two regions
stills.caption: The modal chords
stills.narration: Notice that the third and the sixth, the modal chords, belong to two regions at the same time.

stills.heading: Substitution within a region
stills.caption: Without changing the harmonic sense
stills.narration: Chords of the same region can substitute for each other without changing the harmonic sense of a passage.

stills.heading: Tonality
stills.caption: Relationships, functions and hierarchies around the tonic
stills.narration: Finally, let's talk about tonality. We call tonality the set of relationships, functions and hierarchies that all the sounds of our musical system adopt around one of them, which we choose as the tonal center and call the tonic.

stills.heading: Modulating
stills.caption: Replacing one tonal center with another
stills.narration: To modulate is to replace one tonal center with another. We will study it later.

stills.heading: Accidentals show the key
stills.narration: The altered, or unaltered, notes of a passage tell us its key. If we order the keys by the order in which new accidentals appear, we discover a fixed relationship of perfect fifths.

stills.heading: Order of sharps
stills.caption: F · C · G · D · A · E · B
stills.narration: Sharps appear in this order: F, C, G, D, A, E and B.

stills.heading: Each one a perfect fifth above
stills.narration: Each one is a perfect fifth above the previous one.

stills.heading: Order of flats
stills.caption: B · E · A · D · G · C · F
stills.narration: Flats appear in the opposite order: B, E, A, D, G, C and F.

stills.heading: Each one a perfect fifth below
stills.narration: Each one is a perfect fifth below the previous one.

stills.heading: The circle of fifths
stills.narration: With this we build the circle of fifths.

stills.heading: C major
stills.caption: No accidentals
stills.narration: At the top is C major, with no accidentals.

stills.heading: A fifth above: one more sharp
stills.narration: Going clockwise, each key is a perfect fifth above the previous one and adds a sharp: G, D, A, E, B, F sharp and C sharp.

stills.heading: A fifth below: one more flat
stills.narration: Going counterclockwise, each key is a perfect fifth below and adds a flat: F, B flat, E flat, A flat, D flat, G flat and C flat.

stills.heading: Three enharmonic pairs
stills.caption: Same sound, different spelling
stills.narration: At the bottom of the circle, three positions have two names. B and C flat, F sharp and G flat, C sharp and D flat sound the same, but they are written with different key signatures.

stills.heading: Fifteen major keys
stills.narration: In total we have fifteen major keys.

stills.heading: Relative minors
stills.caption: A minor third below, same key signature
stills.narration: Each key signature also serves a minor key, its relative, a minor third below.

stills.heading: A minor · E minor · D minor
stills.caption: Relatives of C, G and F major
stills.narration: A minor is the relative of C major. E minor, of G major. And D minor, of F major.

stills.heading: Thirty keys
stills.narration: This gives us fifteen minor keys: thirty keys in total.

stills.heading: Let's recap
stills.narration: Let's recap.

stills.heading: Names and functions of the degrees
stills.narration: The degrees have names and functions: tonal, modal, secondary and attractive.

stills.heading: Chords in thirds
stills.narration: Chords are built by stacking thirds, from the fifth chord to the thirteenth chord.

stills.heading: The harmonic series
stills.narration: The harmonic series helps us understand how harmonies changed throughout history.

stills.heading: Tonal regions
stills.narration: The chords of a scale are grouped into the subdominant, tonic and dominant regions.

stills.heading: The circle of fifths
stills.narration: And the circle of fifths organizes the thirty keys.

stills.heading: Next lesson
stills.caption: The vocal quartet: soprano · alto · tenor · bass
stills.narration: In the next lesson we will start writing for the vocal quartet: soprano, alto, tenor and bass.

stills.heading: Thank you
stills.caption: See you in lesson 6
stills.narration: Thank you for joining me. See you in lesson six.
